title: Trump tells Congress to cut basic science research by 34%
content:
Tweet
United States President Donald J Trump has asked Congress to cut funding for basic research by more than one-third in the budget year beginning in October, according to an analysis by the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS).
Fiscal year 2026 (FY26) would see the US government’s spending on basic research decline from US$45 billion to US$30 billion. Applied research would fall even more, 38.2%, or US$20 billion, from this year’s figure of US$52 billion, according to the AAAS analysis.
In total, the administration plans to gut America’s research and development budget – the vast majority of which supports research and development at research universities like Harvard, Stanford, Duke, the University of Wisconsin (Madison), and Texas A&M, research institutes, as well as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) – by 22%, from US$198 billion to US$154 billion.
“If adopted by Congress, it [the budget] would curtail the US’s capabilities to compete with countries like China on biomedicine, quantum computing, and artificial intelligence, and run the risk of not reaping the economic benefits from science and engineering that lead to innovations,” Joanne Padróne Carney , chief government relations officer at the AAAS, told Chemistry World.
She said the proposed cuts for research and development are “unprecedented” and would “bring basic and applied research back to levels not seen since the late 1990s”, when taking inflation into account.
Sudip Parikh, CEO of AAAS, and executive publisher of the Science family of journals in May warned that Trump’s budget request would “end America’s global scientific leadership”.
Iron-clad grip on Congress
The key question is whether Trump's demands will be passed.
While it is an old saw in Washington that when it comes to budgets “The President proposes but Congress disposes,” meaning, because Congress holds the power of the purse, it is supposed to have the last word, given Trump’s iron-clad grip on the slim Republican majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, the normal rules may not apply.
In just the past few weeks, despite paper-thin majorities in both houses of Congress, Trump muscled through the so-called ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ that cut US$1 trillion from Medicare, in order to help fund huge tax cuts for America’s wealthiest corporations and people like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, and a recission package, that codified cuts Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” made to the National Institute of Health, National Science Foundation and USAID.
“In the normal course of budget negotiations, Congress usually significantly modifies presidential budget proposals.
“This was the case in the first Trump administration which proposed in each of its four years large scale cuts to the NIH and NSF and other agencies that fund basic research at American universities,” said John Aubrey Douglass, senior research fellow and research professor – public policy and higher education at the Center for Studies in Higher Education at the University of California, Berkeley.
“But in an era of a thin but meaningful Republican control of both the House and Senate, and their deep fealty to Trump and fear of political and other forms of retribution, Congress earlier showed a willingness to proceed with his plans for draconian cuts to federally funded science, both basic and applied.”
Cuts to every agency
Trump is calling for cuts to every agency and department, with some of the heaviest falling on the NIH and National Science Foundation (NSF).
At the NIH , where Secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F Kennedy Jr plans on firing 20,000 employees, some divisions, including Nursing and Minority Health-Disparities have been eliminated. Funding is planned to decrease by 42%, with research into cancer, allergies, and infectious diseases (by the Center for Disease Control, which oversees COVID vaccines), neuroscience and brain research, child and women’s health are all being cut by approximately 40%. Washington plans on spending 56% less at the NSF, with research declining by 54%. Support for STEM education – including K-12 teacher training and undergraduate scholarships and graduate fellowships and postdoctoral programs – is slated to decline by 75%. Further, the House of Representatives committee considering the budget has recommended ‘zeroing out’ funding for NSF STEM education, meaning eliminating the budget entirely; they have made the same recommendation for STEM education in NASA’s budget. While Trump has asked Congress to increase the research portion of the Department of Defence’s (DoD) budget by 26.3%, basic and applied research being cut by 15% (to US$2 billion) and 18% to US$5.9 billion, respectively. DoD has requested almost 30% less money, or US$397 million less, for basic research by the Air Force and 6.3% (for a total of $578 million) for the Navy’s basic research programmes. The Defense Agencies, which include the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), will lose US$153 million, or 25% of its FY2025 budget of US$768 million. The cuts to DARPA will directly impact universities because, according to Professor Rodney H Yager Jr, who teaches economics at George Mason University, 18% of DARPA’s research budget is spent at research universities. For example, DARPA’s Assured Microbial Preservation in Harsh or Remote Areas (AMPHORA) programme is at Harvard, Duke, and other universities. Researchers in these universities, including graduate students, are working “to develop a portable, cold-chain free system (that is, without refrigeration) that can preserve any microbe (bacteria, fungus, virus) from any sample, environment, or clinical setting”. If successful, the technologies the university researchers develop will increase DoD’s ability to judge environmental threats to military personnel operating anywhere in the world, explained Professor Nicholas G Evans , who teaches philosophy at University of Massachusetts (Lowell) and is the author of The Ethics of Neuroscience and National Security (2021), which examines DARPA’s neuroscience research projects . If enacted, these cuts: “would do little more than smooth the path for China and other competitors as they aggressively ramp up investment to eclipse the US in science and technology investment. In the face of China’s enormous commitment to research and development, the president’s budget represents a surrender of our leadership role”, said Mary Wooley , president and CEO of the advocacy group, Research!America, in a news release. Indicators of resistance In parliamentary democracies because budgets are confidence measures, debates over them tend to be short and have a predetermined outcome. In the US, by contrast, the final vote on the budget is not likely until Congress reconvenes in September from its summer recess. During this period, opponents to specific measures will be lobbying representatives and senators seeing their support to change line items in the budget. According to Douglass: “There are some indicators of resistance to Trump’s proposed cuts to the NSF and NASA in both House and Senate appropriations hearings, in part over fears of the huge impact it would have on the nation’s scientific prowess and competitiveness with economic rivals. “There are twelve appropriation bills that fund other agencies, like the NIH, offering the hope of avoiding a drastic decline in the nation’s science investment. “But will fealty to Trump and desires to cut the federal budget to help pay for tax cuts ultimately win the support of Republicans?”

title: Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ win in EU budget proposals
content:
Tweet
The European research and higher education communities were celebrating some significant wins in the hard-fought battle to get the European Commission to propose big increases in both the draft budgets for the next Horizon Europe research and innovation Framework Programme and the Erasmus+ student mobility scheme.
However, there is a clear air of realism that these are just early victories, and there is uncertainty about the strings attached to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposed budget, which would be worth €2 trillion for the 2028 to 2034 period – and include €175 billion (US$203.91 billion) for research and innovation and €40 billion for Erasmus+.
The figures were only agreed upon by the different Commissioners after late-night, last-minute tweaking, and the final version of “a dynamic EU budget for the priorities of the future” – or the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028 to 2034, to give it the official title – was presented on Wednesday 16 July 2025.
Two years of haggling ahead
The proposals now face two years of haggling between the European Parliament, which will be pressing for more money, and member states on the Council of the European Union, which will be hoping to cut back the proposed increases.
The ambition is to get agreement from all sides before the end of 2027.
The current EU Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2021 to 2027 was set at €1.2 trillion – but on top of that, the EU agreed to invest €806.9 billion in today’s prices in a NextGenerationEU recovery plan (which is helping to pay for post-Covid pandemic recovery and emergency assistance to Ukraine).
The next Framework Programme (FP10), the tenth for research and innovation, will again be called Horizon Europe and remains a standalone budget, which European researchers had been demanding, and University World News has reported.
However, while not being fully absorbed in a new European Competitiveness Fund, or ECF, it will be “working in synergy” with the new over-arching £409 billion ECF mega fund.
Horizon Europe is earmarked to receive €175.3 billion from the ECF pot, with Defence and Space getting €130.7 billion; Clean Transition and decarbonisation €67.4; €54.8 for Digital Transition; and €22.6 billion for Health and bio-economy.
In the current MFF 2021 to 2027, Horizon Europe was given a budget of €95.5 billion. The Commission originally proposed a budget of over €100 billion for the last Framework Programme for research and innovation (which ends in 2027), but this was cut in the last round of tough negotiations over the previous EU budget – and trimmed back to €93.5 billion after a midterm review.
Zaharieva congratulated
Professor Kurt Deketelare, secretary-general of the League of European Research Universities (LERU), congratulated Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, for fighting hard for an increase in the amount earmarked for the next Horizon Europe programme.
Writing on LinkedIn (with a picture of him with Commissioner Zaharieva), Deketelare wrote: “When we last spoke in March, I never would have imagined she could steer the precarious FP10 and MFF debate toward what’s now on the table. Hats off, Commissioner – truly impressive!
Deketelare told University World News that in the detailed communications on the final budget proposals, the Commission plans that Horizon Europe will have four pillars:
• Pillar 1 for Excellence Science (including the European Research Council; Marie Sklodowska-Curie Actions and Joint Research Centre).
• Pillar 2 for Competitiveness and society.
• Pillar 3 Innovation (Including European Innovation Council and Innovation ecosystems).
• Pillar 4 for European (including R&I systems; Research and technology infrastructure and Widening participation).
Deketelare said pillars 1, 3 and 4 are “broadly acceptable”, though he questioned the reduced term of the European Research Council president and is concerned about increasing “directionality” in the Marie Skodowska-Curie Actions.
Horizon pillar 2 ‘lacks transparency’
However, he claimed that pillar 2, covering Competitiveness and Society, “lacks transparency”, especially regarding how its research and innovation activities relate to the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF).
He also questioned the proposed legal framework governing the ECF, saying: “The ‘tight connection’ between Horizon Europe and the ECF remains opaque in terms of a single rulebook, work programmes, funding mechanisms, and governance. “One wonders why such a connection is needed at all – and whether its intended objectives couldn’t simply be achieved through Horizon Europe.” Deketelare is also disappointed that rules for association to the programme remain unchanged, particularly for near neighbouring countries like the United Kingdom and Switzerland, which he said deserve a fast-track association procedure. “Of course, the UK is only associated to this programme, [which finishes at] the end of 2027,” he said. “For the new Horizon Europe they will have to apply again. And I don’t want them to go through the whole complicated association procedure again but give them a fast track,” he said. South Korea has just become the latest, and the first Asian country, to become an associate member of Horizon Europe, which the European Union announced on 17 July 2025. A lot to clarify Deketelare told University World News: “The Commission has now put its proposals on the table. It is up to the Parliament and the Council to formulate their positions. “The Commission’s proposals offer a good starting point, and we count on Parliament and Council to improve them where necessary”. Professor Jan Palmowski, secretary-general of The Guild of European Research Universities, said: “There is much to welcome, but still a lot to clarify” in the European Commission’s budget proposals. He said: “Given what we had been led to expect just a few months ago, many of the broad lines in this proposal are positive: but the devil is in the detail, and a lot of detail is currently missing!” He expanded his concerns about the planned “Missions and Moonshots” in a blog on LinkedIn, but agreed Commission Zaharieva and her team had “done a remarkable job to ensure that this Horizon Europe proposal, for all its gaps and ambiguities, marks a positive start to what will be intense, and hugely important, discussions for the future of Europe”. Erasmus+ The European University Association (EUA), which represents universities and national rectors’ conferences in 48 European countries, welcomed the commitment to retain Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ as stand-alone programmes – and noted that the Erasmus+ budget is earmarked to increase from €26 billion in the last MFF to €40.8 billion in the proposals for the 2028 to 2034 MFF. EUA Secretary General Amanda Crowfoot said: “The proposed increase in Horizon Europe’s budget demonstrates strong support for research and innovation’s essential role in shaping Europe’s future.” However, she said the picture is less clear about Erasmus+, and more information was needed “on how the budget will be allocated across sectors and actions, and how synergies with other EU funding instruments will be implemented”. The EUA pointed out that the Erasmus+ budget, as proposed, will “now need to cover the European Solidarity Corps, which was not previously part of the programme, as well as outgoing international mobility, previously paid by the ‘Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument’ funds”. Other notable additions include dedicated student mobilities for joint programmes and more ‘directional funding’ for scholarships in strategic educational fields. While welcoming “the continued integration of European Universities alliances, one of the most ambitious forms of transnational university cooperation, within the Erasmus programme”, the EUA said: “It is important that the alliances have the freedom to develop their own academic mission without excessive top-down direction.” The new proposed EU budget also envisages a new €9 billion Agora programme to support Europe’s cultural, creative, audiovisual, and media sectors, particularly against the fierce competition and challenges from abrod related to disinformation and decreasing media pluralism and the increased role of online platforms.
